name: Vera Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive my dad's old estate car, which he passed down when he got a new one. I do takeaway and small parcels through one app around our town and the farms outside it. Fridays and Saturdays are fish and chips and curries, weekdays are mostly parcels from the depot by the old cattle market. I'm still learning the farm tracks; last week I left a parcel at the wrong barn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people know me. Old Mrs Ellery from the chapel always says God bless when I bring her shopping. The hard part is the pay, and the car eats petrol on those lanes. I'm engaged to Mark, who's a mechanic at the garage on the high street, and we're trying to save for the wedding next autumn, but we've got barely a month between us. I don't touch the AI stuff on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it. People got carried away. Folks round here like a real person at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life carries on, which I'd welcome. But that doesn't mean easy. Petrol's up, the app pays less on the long farm runs, and the wedding fund keeps getting raided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and take every Saturday shift I can. I'd ask the chip shop owner if she'd pay me direct for local runs. Mark and I would trim the wedding back a bit, smaller reception at the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the robots. Worried about the money, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're saving for the wedding. How is that going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. We had the car tyres and Mark's dentist bill this year. Every time my fiancé Mark and I get a bit of money together, something comes along and takes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got tight, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my mum and dad, and then the chapel. That's how it's always been round here. I don't want a handout from anyone, but I'd take help from people who know me.

say: I **never trusted** AI, and people got carried away.
Folks round here like a **real person** at the door.
think: Life carrying on is welcome, but **not easy** on my pay.
Petrol and **shrinking app pay** keep raiding the wedding fund.
do: Take every **Saturday shift** she can get.
Ask the **chip shop** owner about paid local runs.
Trim the wedding to a **church hall** reception.
feel: **Relieved** about robots, worried about money as always.
S0.quote: Every time my fiancé Mark and I get a bit of money together, something comes along and takes it.
fieldNote: Traditional and **community-minded**: family and chapel come before any public help.
The **wedding fund** is her emotional stake and keeps being spent.
Her worry is **petrol and pay**, not technology.

steps.text: Take every Saturday takeaway shift on the app
Ask the chip shop owner to pay her direct for local runs
Move the wedding reception to the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got along fine without it, and we'll keep going. If the big firms want to change everything, that's their business, but it shouldn't come at the cost of folks' livelihoods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I'm worried about the app. If it gets smarter, it'll pay us less and judge us harder. And I'm slow on the farm tracks, so I'd come off badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down. I'd ask my uncle about work at his feed shop in case the app gets worse. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like I'm being watched by something I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes over planning and answering customers. Do you feel that in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The customer messages would come from a machine, so when I'm late on the lanes, there's nobody to explain it to. My rating would drop and I'd get fewer orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mark's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's fine, I think. Nobody's fixing a gearbox with a computer, and that's the one thing that makes me feel better about my fiancé's job.

say: Folks got along **fine without it** and will keep going.
Big firms' changes shouldn't cost people their **livelihoods**.
think: A smarter app will **pay less** and judge drivers harder.
Being slow on **farm tracks** means I'd come off badly.
do: Keep **driving** and keep her head down.
Ask her uncle about work at his **feed shop**.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if watched by something unseen.
S1.quote: Nobody's fixing a gearbox with a computer, and that's the one thing that makes me feel better about my fiancé's job.
fieldNote: She expects thinking AI to reach her through **app ratings**, not tasks.
Takes comfort in her fiancé's **hands-on trade**.
Her **faith** is part of how she copes.

steps.text: Keep driving the takeaway and parcel rounds
Ask her uncle about a job at his feed shop
Lean on the chapel and family for advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a few big companies get too much power. It's wrong. People need work, not a cheque in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and then robots three years after. My job is the hands-on sort, so I've got until about 2031. Then I'm done, and maybe Mark too if robots learn to fix cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle for a job at the feed shop straight away, before everyone else does. I'd keep the app going on weekends. Mark and I would bring the wedding forward and do it small, so we're married whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep thinking about Mrs Ellery and who'd bring her shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives first and robots around 2031. What would those years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to get into something more solid. The feed shop is hands-on too, lifting sacks and serving farmers. I'd hope that lasts a bit longer, but I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring the wedding forward, register office and a meal at the pub. Getting married before robots take my job matters more to me than a big white dress.

say: Too much power for **a few big companies** is wrong.
People need **work**, not a cheque in the post.
think: My hands-on job lasts until about **2031**, then I'm done.
My fiancé Mark could follow if robots **learn to fix cars**.
do: Ask her uncle for a **feed shop job** straight away.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
feel: **Frightened**, worrying who'd bring her elderly customers their shopping.
S2.quote: Getting married before robots take my job matters more to me than a big white dress.
fieldNote: She blames **concentrated corporate power** rather than government.
Uses the **three-year gap** to move into her uncle's feed shop.
Rejects **handouts**, wanting real work and a steady wage instead.

steps.text: Ask her uncle for a job at his feed shop
Keep weekend takeaway shifts on the app
Marry Mark at the register office within a year
Rely on her parents if money runs short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before. We need to look after our own, family and community, and expect the companies to play fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me until about 2034 on the robots. That's long enough to get settled somewhere. But the app would get worse long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about the feed shop, but take my time. Mark and I would keep the wedding date and save harder. I'd keep driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. Not as frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still rush the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd keep next autumn. My mum's already booked the chapel for next autumn, so the wedding stays. I'd just cut back elsewhere, no takeaways ourselves and no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning any of the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't trust it. If I have to, someday, I'd have Mark show me, but I'm not going to start using it on my own.

say: Communities should **look after their own**, with family coming first.
Big companies must be expected to **play fair** with workers.
think: Robots come around **2034**, which is long enough to get settled elsewhere.
The **app would worsen** long before then, squeezing my pay.
do: Ask about the **feed shop** job without rushing.
Keep the **wedding date** and save harder.
S3.quote: My mum's already booked the chapel for next autumn, so the wedding stays.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **keep tradition**: the chapel wedding stays.
Still refuses **AI tools** unless her fiancé shows her.
She expects to **lose her app income**, keeping her alarmed.

steps.text: Ask her uncle about the feed shop within the year
Stop buying takeaways and skip the holiday
Keep driving the takeaway and parcel rounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no need for panic or government schemes. People should get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd probably just carry on for a while. I'd be married, maybe with a little one on the way. I'd want to be in a steadier job before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the app for now, and look for work at the feed shop or the bakery within a couple of years. Mark and I would save for a deposit on a little house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but the money worries don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to settle down properly. Married, a house maybe, a baby. Ten years is long enough to do it the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your real worry, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money now. The app pays less every year and the car is getting old. Ten years doesn't fix this month's petrol.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, so there's no need for panic.
People should **get on with it** rather than wait for government schemes.
think: With a decade, I'd **carry on** with the app for a while.
I want a **steadier job** before any children arrive.
do: Look for work at the **feed shop or bakery** within two years.
Save for a **house deposit** with Mark.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't fix this month's petrol.
fieldNote: Long warning lets her plan a **traditional life path**: marriage, house, baby.
Current **petrol and pay** keep her anxious.

steps.text: Keep driving for the app for now
Apply at the feed shop or bakery within two years
Save towards a deposit on a small house
Plan a baby after moving to steadier work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of work just as Mark and I are starting out. What would help is local firms getting support to keep people on, and apprenticeships for young people round here, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old folk. Half my parcels go to people who live alone. A robot leaves the box on the step, but a person notices when the curtains haven't opened.

headlineQuote: A robot leaves the box on the step, but a person notices when the curtains haven't opened.
portrait: Vera is **27**, drives her dad's old estate car for one app around a small farming town.
She's **engaged to Mark**, a mechanic, and their wedding fund keeps getting spent.
She avoids **AI tools** and leans on family and chapel rather than government.
Fast AGI pushes her to **marry sooner** and seek work at her uncle's feed shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing work just as she and Mark start married life.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **local firms** to keep staff, and **apprenticeships** for young people.
